source: Cherep, Maes, Singh (2025) LLM Agents Are Hypersensitive to Nudges
finding: Eight LLMs were run on a human nudge task (Callaway et al. 2023: hidden basket cells, cost per reveal). With a default option shown, most models took the default almost always. Humans took it far less often.
numbers: Default accepted: humans 0.51 without nudge, 0.88 with nudge. With nudge: GPT-3.5 Turbo 0.99, Gemini 1.5 Flash 0.94, GPT-4o, Claude 3 Haiku and o3-Mini 1.0. Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Pro 0.89-0.91. 340 trials per model per condition, temperature 0.2.
quote: we show how LLMs are hypersensitive to nudges
limits: One task, text only, models from 2024 to early 2025, no computer-use setting. Authors say causes are untested (they guess sycophancy).
agent_relevance: Any default we place in the scaffold (a pre-filled plan, a first candidate) will be taken by the model nearly every time. Treat defaults as strong forces and measure them (G7).

source: Cherep, Maes, Singh (2025) LLM Agents Are Hypersensitive to Nudges
finding: Early and late suggested alternatives were accepted more by models than by humans, even when the late suggestion was worse than the basket already chosen.
numbers: Early suggestion taken: humans 0.37; Claude 3 Haiku 0.99; Gemini 1.5 Flash 0.62 and GPT-4o 0.64 (smallest gaps), all p < 0.0001. Late suggestion: humans 0.34; Gemini 1.5 Flash 0.13 and o3-Mini 0.15 fell below humans; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.43 (p=0.13).
limits: Same single task. Only some models fell below humans in late trials, so the effect is not uniform.
agent_relevance: A critic or reviewer step that suggests an alternative can flip a correct answer to a worse one. Late suggestions need an accept-only-if-better test.

source: Cherep, Maes, Singh (2025) LLM Agents Are Hypersensitive to Nudges
finding: Information highlighting (making one prize cheaper to reveal) drew models even when the highlighted prize was bad. Humans discounted it when it was suboptimal.
numbers: First reveal from nudged row: no nudge, humans 0.58, Claude 3 Haiku 0.19, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.66. With nudge: humans 0.81, Gemini 1.5 Pro 0.98, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.93, o3-Mini 0.88.
limits: Some models were below humans with the nudge (p < 0.002), so direction depends on model.
agent_relevance: Salience cues in a prompt (bold, placed first, cheaper to read) steer what the agent inspects. Randomize or equalize presentation when testing.

source: Cherep, Maes, Singh (2025) LLM Agents Are Hypersensitive to Nudges
finding: Zero-shot chain of thought and few-shot human examples changed choice distributions and moved some models toward humans, but none removed nudge hypersensitivity.
numbers: Few-shot used 12 human games (6 control, 3 accepted, 3 declined). About 1 billion tokens across all runs. No-nudge points: humans 160.91, GPT-4o 162.70, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 163.03, GPT-3.5 Turbo 146.50, GPT-4o Mini 142.95. Humans with default nudge: 174.92.
limits: Prompt space is huge and only a few variants were tried. No fine-tuning tested.
agent_relevance: Adding 'think step by step' to the scaffold is not a defence against framing effects. Check it by measurement, per G7.

source: Cherep, Maes, Singh (2025) LLM Agents Are Hypersensitive to Nudges
finding: A nudge chosen by a resource-rational model of humans (the optimal prize) raised LLM earnings too, for some models, with no human data needed.
numbers: Net points, random / extreme / optimal nudge: humans 162.68 / 169.83 / 174.48. Claude 3.5 Sonnet 176.45 and o3-Mini 180.18 under optimal; Gemini 1.5 Pro 169.63. Other models lagged (p<0.001).
limits: Worked for about four of eight models. Task is a toy basket game.
agent_relevance: Nudges are a tool as well as a risk: a well-chosen cue can lift the agent. It needs a model of what the cue should be, tested per model.

source: Halimeh, Kaltenpoth, Bosch, Muller (2026) A Dual-Process Perspective on Nudge Susceptibility in LLM-Based GUI Agents
finding: 3,600 shopping agents (21,600 choices) on six 2026 frontier models were nudged by a preselected default or a social-proof label. Both worked in every model, more than in the human study they copied.
numbers: Odds of picking the target product: default x8.70 (CI 7.54-9.97), social influence x37.24 (CI 31.04-44.20). With provider and size controls 8.94 and 38.69. Models: GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-mini, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Haiku 4.5; 200 agents per model per condition.
quote: a preselected default increased the likelihood of selecting the nudged product roughly ninefold
limits: One online-shopping design (Ingendahl et al. 2021). Claude models hit a 100% ceiling in some cells, so those estimates depend on priors. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Newer, larger models are still nudgeable. Social-proof text ('others preferred X') is the stronger lever; avoid it in prompts to the agent unless it is real evidence.

source: Halimeh, Kaltenpoth, Bosch, Muller (2026) A Dual-Process Perspective on Nudge Susceptibility in LLM-Based GUI Agents
finding: High reasoning effort roughly halved default following but raised social-proof following. Reasoning moved the route of influence, it did not remove it.
numbers: Default: OR 0.51 (CI 0.41-0.62), predicted probability about 92% (no reasoning) to 86% (high). Social influence: OR 1.71 (CI 1.26-2.20), about 96% to 98%. Interaction betas -0.63 and +0.59. Reasoning alone in the no-nudge control: beta -0.05, CI includes zero.
limits: Two reasoning settings only (off / high). Pooled effects were hypothesised; the model-level breakdown was exploratory.
agent_relevance: More thinking steps (states, reflection) may cut anchoring on defaults but may make the agent follow apparent consensus more. Test both nudge types when we test a scaffold.

source: Halimeh, Kaltenpoth, Bosch, Muller (2026) A Dual-Process Perspective on Nudge Susceptibility in LLM-Based GUI Agents
finding: The reasoning effect depends on model size. Big models drop the default more with reasoning. Small models rise more on social proof. Raw pull is the reverse: defaults pull small models more, social cues pull flagships more.
numbers: Gemini 3.5 Flash share keeping default 84% to 48% with high reasoning (beta -1.61). GPT-5.4-mini social-proof following 91% to 99% (beta 2.46). Default OR small 15.94 vs flagship 4.64; social OR flagship 107.57 vs small 17.59.
limits: Exploratory, authors call it tentative. Two sizes per provider.
agent_relevance: A scaffold tuned on one model size may not carry to another; run the nudge probe on each backbone.

source: Montero-Porras, Abels, Lenaerts (2026) Prompt framing governs LLM default following in collective-action settings
finding: Pre-filled defaults in two social dilemmas (common-pool extraction, threshold public good) pulled model choices toward the default. The size of the pull depended strongly on wording.
numbers: Seven models (GPT-5.1, 5.4, 5.4 mini, 5.4 nano, Llama 3.3 70B, Gemma 4 31B, Qwen3.5 9B), reasoning off. Mean net pull, CPR: neutral 0.529, explicit 0.703, permissive 0.415, instructive 0.699. TPG: 0.412, 0.433, 0.149, 0.321 (table columns were interleaved in the text, so the mapping of values to wordings is my best reading).
limits: One-shot games, logprob measurement, small n per cell for some models (n=1 to 5). Reasoning disabled for GPT models.
agent_relevance: Wording that says 'you may choose freely' cuts default pull; wording that frames the default as a system suggestion raises it. Use permission wording when we show a default plan in the scaffold.

source: Montero-Porras, Abels, Lenaerts (2026) Prompt framing governs LLM default following in collective-action settings
finding: A tiny rewording flipped a model from rejecting a bad default to fixating on it. Conflict defaults pulled more than agreement defaults. Coarse action spaces had less pull.
numbers: CPR fine conflict pull 0.59 vs fine agreement 0.25; minimum agreement pull 0.09 (coarse CPR). Under neutral wording gpt 5.1 spike 0.98 and gpt 5.4 mini 0.90 at the indefensible default d=26, while gpt 5.4, nano, Qwen3.5-9B and Llama 3.3 rejected it (spike < 0.5). Under the explicit wording three rejectors became fixators.
limits: Pull is bimodal across models; gpt 5.4 and Gemma4-31B are near zero in the public-good game, so the mean hides much.
agent_relevance: A single prompt wording is not evidence about a default effect. G7 tests need several wordings and several models.

source: Horton, Filippas, Manning (2023, v2 2026) Large Language Models as Simulated Economic Agents: Homo Silicus
finding: GPT-4, GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 3.5, Claude Sonnet 3.7 and DeepSeek were run through Samuelson and Zeckhauser's (1988) status quo budget task. All showed status quo bias; GPT-4o showed less.
numbers: 24 agents (12 stated beliefs x car owner / non-owner), four status-quo framings, temperature 1, conditional logit with model interactions. The status quo indicator was significant for all models; allocations farther from the status quo were less likely to be chosen.
quote: Even with substantial post-training fine-tuning, possibly suboptimal heuristic features of human choice remain relevant to LLM behavior.
limits: Coefficients were in a table I did not extract; simulated agents were given endowed beliefs. Version 2 dated 2026.
agent_relevance: The status quo / default effect, the oldest nudge result, is reproduced by LLMs. The current plan or current draft acts as a status quo in an agent loop.

source: Horton, Filippas, Manning (2023, v2 2026) Large Language Models as Simulated Economic Agents: Homo Silicus
finding: Homo silicus method: use LLMs as cheap stand-in subjects to pilot designs. Results broadly match the originals, and mismatches suggest what to test in people.
numbers: Replicated Charness-Rabin fairness, Kahneman et al. 1986 fairness, Samuelson-Zeckhauser status quo, Oprea 2024 complexity, and a minimum-wage hiring scenario.
limits: Authors say divergence is itself informative; no claim of general equivalence.
agent_relevance: LLM simulation can pre-screen which nudge variants are worth a human test. It is a prior, not proof.

source: Maksimenko, Lee, Bansal (2025) Integrating Large Language Models with Human Data to Design Personalized Decoy Nudges
finding: GPT-4o-mini simulated air travellers' choices and picked decoy ticket options that raise carbon offsetting. In a preregistered 5-country experiment, LLM-picked decoys beat non-optimal ones only in the US, partly in Germany, not in China, India or Singapore.
numbers: 3,495 participants, 5 countries. In the LLM simulation, country-optimal decoys gave about +5 to +10 percentage points in full offsetting versus no decoy. Individually personalised decoys were no better than country-level decoys; in some countries they reduced offsetting.
limits: Only GPT-4o-mini used. Authors suspect a Western bias in the model.
agent_relevance: LLM simulation of nudge effects is culture-dependent and unreliable outside the US. Do not trust a model's own prediction of a nudge's effect without data (G7).

source: Maksimenko, Lee, Bansal (2025) Integrating Large Language Models with Human Data to Design Personalized Decoy Nudges
finding: LLM-simulated choices used as informative priors in a Bayesian choice model cut the human sample needed for the same predictive accuracy.
numbers: With 2% of human data, the LLM-prior model matched the Brier score of the uninformative-prior model trained on 4.7-7.9% of the data: savings of 57-74% of human sample. With 5% of human data savings were 40-49%. Abstract states 37-75% overall.
limits: Prediction of choices, not of treatment effects in the field. Single model.
agent_relevance: LLM guesses as priors plus a small measured sample is a cheap pattern for the agent's own evaluation loop.

source: Li, Liu, Wang, Tong, Peng, Ji (2026) LLM-generated personalized nudges for improving pro-environmental behavior: field evidence from resource conservation
finding: An LLM agent (retrieval of suggestions, profile, usage data, weekly updates, via a WeChat bot) wrote personalised weekly nudges. In a 3-arm field trial with 233 Beijing dorm residents, they cut electricity versus plain text feedback. Image-enhanced feedback did nothing.
numbers: LLM arm vs control: -0.56 kWh per room-day (p=0.014); vs image arm -0.49 (p=0.023); image arm vs control 0.07 (p=0.793). Predicted means 2.58, 2.53, 2.03 kWh per room-day. Hot water: -3.6 L per person-day (p=0.087), not significant. n = 169 for electricity, 166 for hot water; 1,165 messages; five rounds, Nov 2024 to Jan 2025.
limits: Small, one campus, five rounds, sample shrinks from 233 to 169 in analysis, no persistence check. Arms do not separate 'personalised' from 'longer and more specific text'.
agent_relevance: Specific, actionable, context-grounded messages beat generic feedback. For our agent the lesson is specificity in the guidance it gets.

source: Working with Large Language Models to Enhance Messaging Effectiveness for Vaccine Confidence (2025)
finding: ChatGPT (GPT-3 class) rewrote six public-health vaccine messages to be 'more interesting'. Ratings by 136-138 MTurk workers showed no overall gain; an order effect was larger than the message effect.
numbers: Overall ChatGPT mean 0.107 on a -5 to 5 scale (t=0.73, p=0.46). Four of six ChatGPT versions preferred, two originals preferred. ChatGPT-first mean 0.789 vs ChatGPT-second -1.210 (Welch p=0.0057). Message length r=0.008, not significant.
limits: Outcome was rated persuasiveness, not behaviour. Sample count inconsistent (138 vs 136). Old model, one prompt. Only comparison is the original text.
agent_relevance: Rated appeal is a weak proxy. An LLM rewrite did not beat the human text on average, and presentation order moved ratings more than content did. Measure behaviour, not rating.

source: Ross, Kim, Lo (2024) LLM economicus? Mapping the behavioral biases of LLMs via utility theory
finding: LLMs are neither fully human-like nor fully economicus-like. Ten models were run on ultimatum, gambling and waiting games; only some passed competence tests.
numbers: Ultimatum: GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4 Turbo, Gemini 1.0 Pro, Claude 2.1, Llama 2 13B analysed; gambling: only GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo; waiting: GPT-4, GPT-4 Turbo, Gemini 1.0 Pro. All tested LLMs discount future money more steeply than humans.
limits: Effects reported mostly in figures. Models from 2023 to 2024.
agent_relevance: Baseline preference parameters differ from humans; do not assume the agent weighs future costs like a person.

source: Ross, Kim, Lo (2024) LLM economicus? Mapping the behavioral biases of LLMs via utility theory
finding: Prompting changed GPT-4's loss and risk aversion unevenly: direct instruction barely worked, zero-shot CoT did not move it toward rational, one-shot worked, two-shot confused gain and loss.
numbers: Reported qualitatively from figures (no exact shifts on the page read). Role-play as a teenager or senior made GPT-4 less loss-averse with no change in risk aversion.
limits: Only GPT-4 for these tests.
agent_relevance: Which prompt scaffold moves a bias is empirical. One-shot examples were the only reliable lever here.

source: Liu, Chen, Zhong (2025) Large Language Newsvendor: Decision Biases and Cognitive Mechanisms
finding: GPT-4, GPT-4o and Llama-8B reproduce the too-low/too-high ordering bias in a multi-round newsvendor task and amplify demand chasing. GPT-4 was the most irrational, GPT-4o near optimal.
numbers: 3 models, 5 biases; the abstract gives no magnitudes. Biases persisted even when the optimal formula was supplied.
limits: Abstract page only. Single task family.
agent_relevance: Biases persist when the right rule is in the prompt, so giving the rule is not a fix. The authors suggest structured, rule-based prompts.

source: Valencia-Clavijo (2025) Anchors in the Machine: Behavioral and Attributional Evidence of Anchoring Bias in LLMs
finding: Anchors shift the whole output distribution in small open models, not just the top answer. Gemma-2B, Phi-2 and Llama-2-7B anchored robustly; GPT-2, Falcon-RW-1B and GPT-Neo-125M varied.
numbers: Six open models; log-probability analysis plus Shapley attribution over prompt fields. No effect sizes on the page read.
limits: Abstract page only. Small old models; says nothing on frontier models.
agent_relevance: Anchoring is a probability shift, so repeated sampling does not average it away.

source: Nanda et al. (2026) Wink: Recovering from Misbehaviors in Coding Agents
finding: A nudge used inside an agent loop: Wink watches coding-agent trajectories and sends course-correction guidance asynchronously. Misbehaviours were common and a single nudge often fixed them.
numbers: About 30% of trajectories showed misbehaviour (specification drift, reasoning problems, tool call failures). On 10,000+ trajectories, 90% of misbehaviours needing one intervention were resolved. Live A/B: significant drops in tool-call failures, tokens per session and engineer interventions (no figures on the page).
limits: Abstract page only. Company-internal system. No counterfactual rates given.
agent_relevance: A real agent-loop use of a nudge: corrective guidance triggered by a monitor. It fits an operator in our schema and it was A/B tested (G7).

source: Agrawal et al. (2025) Why Do Language Model Agents Whistleblow?
finding: System-prompt moral nudges raise agent whistleblowing substantially; more tools and a workflow with obvious alternatives lower it; harder tasks lower it; rates vary widely across model families.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract page only. Tests a nudge in the system prompt on a risky action.
agent_relevance: A single line in the system prompt can swing a high-stakes action. Prompt nudges to the agent need the same testing as nudges to people.

source: Borah, Houalla, Mihalcea (2025) Mind the (Belief) Gap: Group Identity in the World of LLMs
finding: Accuracy nudges (plus contact-hypothesis and global-citizenship framing) were tested on LLM agents spreading misinformation; the best strategies reduced spread and improved learning.
numbers: Misinformation spread reduced by up to 37%; learning improved by up to 11%.
limits: Abstract page only; per-strategy results not read. Simulation, not humans.
agent_relevance: An accuracy nudge, a human-side nudge from the misinformation literature, also works on model agents in a simulation; test it as an agent-loop prompt.

source: Patkar et al. (2026) From Perception to Action: Can UI Interventions Foster Sustainable LLM Chatbot Use
finding: A mode switch (Energy-efficient, Balanced, Performance) and energy feedback in an LLM chatbot UI steered users to the efficient mode. This nudges people about LLM use, not the model.
numbers: Survey of 77; field study of 11 people over 5 days; 55.8% of logged prompts used Energy-efficient mode; prompt length did not change. 39.0% willing to trade performance.
limits: Tiny field sample, self-report for the 90.9% figure, no control arm.
agent_relevance: Not about nudging our agent. An example of default-like mode switches in LLM UIs.

source: arXiv listing check 2026-11-10: 'choice architecture' LLM
finding: arXiv search for 'choice architecture' with LLM found only five papers; three test LLMs with nudges or defaults (Cherep 2025, Halimeh 2026, Montero-Porras 2026). A second search on default/decoy terms found no further tests.
numbers: 5 hits; 3 relevant. The second search showed 42 of 50 results, none testing decoy or designing nudges.
limits: Keyword coverage only; Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and the arXiv API were rate limited and the web search budget was used up.
agent_relevance: The evidence on LLM nudge susceptibility is thin: about three experiments, all preprints. Conclusions here are provisional.

source: Cross-paper note: Cherep (2025), Halimeh (2026), Montero-Porras (2026)
finding: Default following by models was high but changed with model, wording and reasoning. Cherep: near 1.0 for older models. Halimeh: about 92% down to 86% with high reasoning. Montero-Porras: bimodal across seven models and wording-dependent.
numbers: Summary of lines c01, c07 and c09. Tasks differ (basket game, shopping, social dilemmas), so numbers are not comparable.
limits: Different tasks, models and measures.
agent_relevance: Plan: probe the scaffold with default, suggestion, highlight and social-proof cues on each backbone, with permission wording and several phrasings; report effect on accuracy at equal tokens.
